toc.title: When and How a Project Ends
Determine Criteria to Successfully Close the Project or Phase (ECO)
Obtain Stakeholder Approval of Project Completion (ECO)
Conclude Activities to Close the Project or Phase (ECO)
Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

html:
1Core Concepts and Definitions

Term Meaning
Closing Focus Area The actions that formally complete or close a project, phase or contract, or terminate a project early. It may include verifying that specific actions from the other Focus Areas are done. Its key benefit: phases, projects and contracts are closed out appropriately, transitioning to operations in a way that helps meet or exceed the business objectives
Close Project or Phase The process of finalizing all activities for successful and unsuccessful projects, phases, releases, iterations or contracts: archiving information, completing planned work, releasing resources for new projects, and confirming the extent to which value, or the capability to deliver value, was achieved
Completion (exit) criteria The conditions that must be met before a project or phase can close; agreed early, measurable and documented
Verified deliverable Checked for correctness through quality control (Monitor and Control Scope)
Accepted deliverable Formally accepted by the customer or sponsor through Validate Scope; the input to closing
Final product, service or result transition The handover of what the project produced (or, for a phase, the intermediate result) to a different group that will operate, maintain and support it
Transition readiness The receiver's ability to run the result: people, skills, documents, support, access and acceptance
Final report A summary of project performance, including scope, quality, cost, schedule, benefits and business needs, and the risks and issues met
Administrative closure Closing the project's own records, accounts, resources and documents
Contract closure Formal acceptance of the seller's work, with claims, guarantees, warranties and payments finalized
Lessons learned register and repository The project document of lessons and the OPA that receives it at the end (Topic 31)
Benefits owner The person accountable for monitoring, recording and reporting realized benefits after closure, as set in the benefits management plan
Early termination Closing before the planned schedule or budget is used up, for positive cause (value achieved) or negative cause (value no longer achievable)
Post-implementation review Beyond PMBOK 8 A later check, often by the benefits owner, of whether intended benefits materialized

2When and How a Project Ends

PMBOK 8 (Standard §1.3): a project usually ends when one or more of these hold:

  • the objectives have been achieved;
  • a governing body, the sponsor or the team determines the objectives will not or cannot be met;
  • resources (funding, human or physical) are exhausted or no longer available;
  • changes in strategy, priorities or the external environment mean the need no longer exists;
  • the project is terminated for legal, regulatory or compliance reasons.

Governance scenarios (Table 2-2): early termination for positive cause (the desired value impact was achieved before the schedule or budget was used up) and early termination for negative cause (the desired value impact is no longer achievable). In every case the value proposition is the primary factor (Topic 12). Where canceling is the best way to maximize the return, or to minimize a negative one, the Closing Focus Area also covers suspension or early closure.

Who decides: the sponsor holds decision authority, may propose termination, ensures long-term benefits realization and authorizes project completion (Stakeholders domain); governance bodies decide where the framework says so. The project manager analyzes, recommends and carries out closure.

3The Closure Sequence

Gate ECO enabler What it means
1 Set the criteria Determine criteria to successfully close Agree exit criteria early and keep them current (section 4)
2 Obtain acceptance Obtain stakeholder approval of completion Verified deliverables are formally accepted; vendors' work is accepted (section 5)
3 Validate readiness Validate readiness for transition The receiver can operate or continue the work (section 6)
4 Conclude activities Conclude activities to close Financials, procurement, resources, records, final lessons, final report (section 7)
5 Authorize completion Stakeholder approval The sponsor or governance authorizes closure; stakeholders are informed

If a gate is not passed, fix or renegotiate and check again. Do not close on technical completion, schedule or budget alone.

4Determine Criteria to Successfully Close the Project or Phase (ECO)

  • Define closure criteria early, in the charter, the plan, the contract and the benefits management plan, with the sponsor and customer; revisit them when scope changes. PMBOK 8: the project manager ensures all work is complete and the objectives are met by reviewing the project management plan.
  • Make them measurable and agreed. The business case is used to measure success at the end against the objectives (Topic 09).
Category Typical criteria
Product and scope Deliverables meet the acceptance criteria and are formally accepted by the customer (Topic 15)
Quality and compliance Verification complete; operational acceptance, security, safety and regulatory checks passed (Topic 23)
Administrative Documents updated; all issues resolved (or transferred with owners); all costs charged; project accounts closed; personnel reassigned; facilities and equipment released
Contractual Seller's work accepted; claims, guarantees and warranties finalized; invoices paid; disputes resolved or referred
Transition Receivers trained and equipped; documentation, support and access ready; outstanding risks transferred
Knowledge Lessons learned captured; records audited and archived; OPAs updated
Value Measurable value delivered and a plan to maintain it after closure; benefits owner and metrics set

Three kinds of "done," do not mix them: acceptance criteria (per deliverable), definition of done (per backlog item or increment) and closure criteria (for the project or phase).

  • Phases and gates: each phase has exit criteria and closes with acceptance before the next begins, even if the sponsor stays the same.
  • Adaptive work: confirm that prioritized backlog items are finished and all acceptance criteria are met; stakeholders have reviewed and accepted the deliverables; a final review shows no outstanding issues (PMBOK 8). When funding ends, agree closure criteria and transfer the remaining backlog to the product owner: unfinished value belongs to the product, not the project.
  • Terminated projects: agree the closure criteria with the sponsor when the decision is made (section 8).

5Obtain Stakeholder Approval of Project Completion (ECO)

The chain: verify (quality control checks correctness) → validate and accept (the customer formally accepts against the acceptance criteria) → authorize completion (the sponsor or governance) → inform stakeholders.

  • Passing quality control is not acceptance. Hold a formal acceptance review with the customer or business owner; silence is not acceptance.
  • Who approves: the customer or product owner (deliverables), operations or the receiving owner (transition), the sponsor (authorizes completion), governance bodies where required, regulators or compliance owners where applicable, and vendors (mutual formal acceptance of the seller's work).
  • Document it: a signed acceptance, minutes and a closure notice; formal written acceptance for contracts.
  • If acceptance is refused: record the reasons; fix and re-verify; treat new requests as change requests; escalate disputes; agree open items and owners if a conditional acceptance is used Beyond PMBOK 8; do not close.
  • A new sponsor or key stakeholder must be engaged before closure so completion is accepted by those who now own the outcome (Topic 32).
  • Phases and iterations: acceptance happens at each phase gate, release or iteration review; the final release is accepted against the definition of done and the release criteria.
  • Satisfaction: measure stakeholder satisfaction as part of closing (Topic 13), and tell all stakeholders that the project is closed.

6Validate Readiness for Transition (ECO)

Scope complete is not transition ready. PMBOK 8 requires the final product, service or result to be transitioned to the group that will operate, maintain and support it, with a plan to maintain the value as the project closes.

Check:

  1. People and skills: the receivers have done the work with support, not only watched demonstrations or read manuals.
  2. Documentation and knowledge: operating and support documents; tacit knowledge captured from people who are leaving (shadowing, pairing, hands-on practice; Topic 27).
  3. Support model: service levels, contacts, escalation, warranty or hypercare period Beyond PMBOK 8.
  4. Environment and access: production environment, tools, licenses and access ready; data migrated; cut-over and rollback tested Beyond PMBOK 8.
  5. Verification and compliance: operational acceptance criteria met; performance, security and regulatory checks passed.
  6. Open items and risks: issues, defects and outstanding risks accepted or transitioned to operations, with named owners and plans.
  7. Ownership and benefits: the receiving owner accepts in writing; a benefits owner and metrics are set; budget exists for the run phase.
  8. Communication: users and stakeholders know what changes, when and where to get help.

Rules of thumb:

  • If readiness work (for example training) is incomplete, complete it before the formal handover; do not close the project and leave operations to arrange it.
  • If people who hold critical knowledge are leaving soon, capture the knowledge from them first; documents can be reviewed later.
  • Phase to phase: hand the next phase (or a new contractor) what it needs, after the phase is formally accepted.
  • Oversight may continue after deliverables are finalized but before formal closure, for benefits realization and sustainment (Standard §2.4.1).

7Conclude Activities to Close the Project or Phase (ECO)

7.1 Satisfy the exit criteria (PMBOK 8, predictive)

  • Ensure all documents and deliverables are updated and all issues resolved (Topic 30).
  • Ensure the measurable project value was delivered and there is a plan to maintain it as the project transitions to operations.
  • Confirm that deliverables were delivered and formally accepted by the customer.
  • Verify that all costs have been charged to the project and close project accounts (financial closure; Topic 17).
  • Reassign or release project personnel; address excess project materials; reallocate or release facilities, equipment and other resources (Topic 19).
  • Prepare final project reports as the organization requires.

7.2 Close contractual agreements (Topic 22)

  • Confirm formal acceptance of the external source's work.
  • Finalize open claims, guarantees and warranties; ensure all invoices due are paid.
  • Resolve disputes or refer them to the dispute board.
  • Update records with the final results and archive relevant information.
  • Every contract must be closed before the project is.

7.3 Additional closure activities

  • Collect and audit project or phase records; archive project information for future organizational use (a controlled, accessible repository).
  • Assess project success or failure (against objectives, business case and benefits). PMBOK 8 lists document analysis, regression analysis (how input variables related to outcomes, to improve future projects), trend analysis and variance analysis as the data analysis tools of Close Project or Phase, with expert judgment and meetings (for example lessons learned and retrospective meetings).
  • Manage knowledge sharing and transfer; identify and document lessons learned (a final session for project-level lessons, even if retrospectives ran every iteration; Topic 31).
  • Transfer the product, service or result to the next phase or into production or operations.
  • Collect suggestions for improving or updating organizational policies and procedures and forward them to the appropriate unit; update OPAs.
  • Measure stakeholder satisfaction.
  • Verify that all contractual, regulatory, legal, social and environmental obligations have been met (Topic 23).
  • Identify outstanding risks to accept or transition to operations (Topic 21).

7.4 Final report

The final report summarizes performance: a description of the project or phase; scope objectives and evidence that completion criteria were met; quality objectives, verification and reasons for variances; cost objectives and variances; validation of the final product; schedule objectives; benefits and business needs achieved (or an estimate of when they will be); and the risks and issues met and how they were handled.

7.5 Benefits after closure

The business case and benefits management plan are business documents developed before the project and referenced after it ends. The benefits owner monitors, records and reports realized benefits over the planned timeframe; the project manager hands this over with the metrics and does not stay accountable for benefits indefinitely (Topic 10). Beyond PMBOK 8 A post-implementation review checks later whether the benefits appeared.

8Early Termination and Canceled Projects

  • Triggers are in section 2; governance and the sponsor decide, on the project manager's analysis. Sunk costs are ignored in the decision; finishing only to avoid wasting spent money ignores the decision (Topic 10).
  • A terminated project still closes formally. PMBOK 8 expects procedures to investigate and document the reasons the project was terminated before completion, and to engage the relevant stakeholders.
  • Do: document the work delivered; decide what can be transitioned or reused; settle contracts under their termination provisions (accept and pay for what was delivered, finalize claims); release people and resources; capture lessons; archive records; communicate the decision and its reasons.
  • Positive cause (value achieved): confirm the value with the sponsor, transition what exists, release unused funds.
  • Negative cause: be transparent about why, protect people and relationships, and learn.

9Predictive vs Agile vs Hybrid

Predictive Agile / adaptive Hybrid
Closure unit Phase and project, with gates Iteration, release and product (the project may close while the product continues) Both
Acceptance Formal acceptance against acceptance criteria; sign-off Stakeholder review at each iteration or release against the definition of done; final release review Formal for the baselined parts, review-based for increments
Criteria Exit criteria in plan and contract Definition of done, release criteria; closure criteria agreed when funding ends Both
Knowledge Final lessons session; archive Retrospectives each iteration plus a final session; knowledge-sharing sessions Both
Remaining work Open items transferred with owners Unfinished backlog goes to the product owner Mixed
Risks Outstanding risks accepted or transitioned to operations Risks accepted or passed to subsequent iterations, releases, clients or operations Both

10Tailoring, Interactions and Checking Results

  • Tailor formality to project size, complexity, contract and regulation, number of vendors, transition complexity and organizational record-retention policy: a small internal project may close with one meeting and a short report; a regulated or multi-vendor project needs formal acceptances, audits and contract close-out notices.
  • Interactions: scope and quality (acceptance), procurement (contract closure), finance (accounts), resources (release and recognition), risk and issues (hand-over), stakeholders (satisfaction, approval), knowledge (lessons), governance (authorization, early termination), benefits (owner) and change control (new requests after acceptance become new work).
  • Check results (PMBOK 8): the confirmation that value, or the capability to deliver it, was achieved; deliverables formally accepted; project value maintained through transition. Beyond PMBOK 8practice Healthy signs: signed acceptance on file; closure checklist complete; no unowned issues or risks; contracts closed; records archived; benefits owner and metrics in place; lessons in the repository; team released and recognized.

11Exam Traps and What PMI Expects

  1. Passing tests is not acceptance: obtain formal acceptance from the customer against the acceptance criteria; silence is not acceptance.
  2. Each phase closes formally with acceptance, even with the same sponsor; lessons then feed the next phase.
  3. Scope complete is not transition ready: complete training and readiness work before the formal handover; do not close and leave operations to arrange it.
  4. Financial closure comes before project closure: all costs charged, invoices paid, accounts closed.
  5. Close every contract first: accept the seller's work, finalize claims and warranties, resolve or refer disputes.
  6. A terminated or canceled project still closes formally: document delivered work, reasons and lessons; settle contracts; do not finish only to save sunk costs.
  7. When funding ends in agile work, agree closure criteria and transfer the remaining backlog to the product owner.
  8. Capture knowledge from departing people first; hands-on practice beats demos and manuals.
  9. Hold a final lessons session even if retrospectives ran every iteration; make lessons searchable; update OPAs.
  10. Resolve or transfer every issue and risk with an owner; do not leave them unowned or erase them.
  11. Release and reassign people, address excess materials, and close accounts and facilities.
  12. Archive records in a controlled repository per policy; collect and audit them first.
  13. Verify obligations (contractual, regulatory, legal, social, environmental) are met.
  14. The sponsor or governance authorizes completion, not the project manager alone; engage a new sponsor before closing.
  15. Value and benefits outlast the project: confirm value delivered, name a benefits owner and hand over tracking.
  16. Do not close on schedule and budget alone; confirm the criteria and the value.
  17. New requests after acceptance go through change control as new work, not into the closed scope.

12Exam Q&A

12.1 Scenario questions (choose the best answer)

S1Every story in the last release met the definition of done, so the team declares the project finished, although the contract lists closure criteria that include final documentation and a security sign-off. What should the project manager do?

  • AAdd the closure criteria to the definition of done for the next release
  • BClose the project, because meeting the definition of done means the project is complete
  • CCheck the project's closure criteria separately from the definition of done
  • DTreat the contract's closure criteria as optional once the stories are accepted
Show the answer

Answer: C. Acceptance criteria apply to deliverables, the definition of done to backlog items and increments, and closure criteria to the project or phase, so the three must not be mixed. Closing on the definition of done, ignoring contract criteria or moving them into the next release leaves the project unfinished.

S2A customer refuses to accept an increment, citing two nonconformities and also asking for a new reporting feature. What should the project manager do?

  • AClose the project anyway, since the deliverable was built to the agreed specification
  • BAsk the sponsor to accept the deliverable in place of the customer
  • CAdd the new feature to the deliverable and request acceptance of the whole package
  • DFix and re-verify the nonconformities, and handle the new feature as a change request
Show the answer

Answer: D. When acceptance is refused, the reasons are recorded, nonconformities are fixed and re-verified, and new requests become change requests; the project does not close until acceptance is obtained. Folding the feature in, closing anyway or substituting the sponsor skips the customer's acceptance.

S3Operations has accepted a new system in principle, but no support model, escalation path or hypercare period has been defined. What should the project manager do before the handover?

  • AHand over the system now and let operations create its own support model afterward
  • BKeep the project team on call indefinitely without any agreement for the arrangement
  • CInclude a long support section in the user manual and consider the matter closed
  • DDefine service levels, contacts, escalation and a hypercare period with operations
Show the answer

Answer: D. Transition readiness includes a support model such as service levels, contacts, escalation and a warranty or hypercare period, agreed before the handover. Leaving it to operations, burying it in a manual or an open-ended on-call arrangement does not give the receiver a workable model.

S4At closure, three open risks remain, and the team that owned them is about to disband. What should the project manager do?

  • ALeave the risks in the register with the departing team's names
  • BAccept them formally or transition them to operations with named owners
  • CDelete the risks from the register, since the project is coming to an end
  • DMark all three risks as occurred so that they become issues
Show the answer

Answer: B. Outstanding risks at closure are identified and either accepted or transitioned to operations with named owners and plans. Deleting them, leaving departing owners or relabeling them as issues leaves the exposure unowned.

S5The draft final report for a hybrid project covers only the delivered scope and the final cost. What should the project manager add?

  • AA forecast of the next project that the organization is likely to undertake
  • BOnly the names of the team members and the dates of the main project meetings
  • CQuality, schedule, benefits achieved, and the risks and issues met and handled
  • DA detailed daily log of every activity performed from the start of the project
Show the answer

Answer: C. The final report summarizes performance across scope, quality, cost, schedule, benefits and business needs, and the risks and issues met and how they were handled. Names, an activity log or a forecast of future work do not summarize how the project performed.

S6The sponsor expects the project manager to remain accountable for realizing the benefits for the next two years. What is the correct approach?

  • AHand tracking to a benefits owner with metrics and a timeframe
  • BAccept the accountability, since the business case belongs to the project manager
  • CKeep the project open for two years so that benefits can be tracked by the team
  • DRefuse any involvement and leave the benefits measurement to chance
Show the answer

Answer: A. The benefits owner monitors, records and reports realized benefits over the planned timeframe, and the project manager hands over the metrics rather than staying accountable indefinitely. Keeping the project open, accepting open-ended accountability or refusing all involvement leaves benefits tracking unowned or misplaced.

S7As the project closes, the project manager wants to know whether stakeholders are satisfied with the result. What should be included in the closing activities?

  • AMeasuring stakeholder satisfaction and announcing that the project is closed
  • BSending the sponsor a final invoice and then archiving the stakeholder register
  • CWaiting for complaints to arrive in the months after the project closes
  • DAssuming satisfaction from the fact that the deliverables were accepted
Show the answer

Answer: A. Closing includes measuring stakeholder satisfaction and informing all stakeholders that the project is closed. Acceptance of deliverables does not prove satisfaction, and waiting for complaints or filing the register leaves the question unanswered.

S8A week after the final release was accepted, the customer asks for an additional report in the delivered system. How should the project manager treat the request?

  • AAs a reason to reopen the project and withdraw the customer's acceptance
  • BAs new work to be assessed through change control, not as part of the closed scope
  • CAs a small favor to be done quietly by the team before it disbands
  • DAs a defect to be repaired at the project's expense under the warranty
Show the answer

Answer: B. New requests after acceptance go through change control as new work and are not added to the closed scope. Treating them as defects, doing them quietly or reopening the project ignores the formal acceptance.

S9Operations says it has no budget to run and support the new system after handover. What should the project manager do?

  • ARaise it with the sponsor before handover, since run-phase budget is part of readiness
  • BDelay the closure silently while hoping that operations finds funds
  • CUse the remaining project budget to fund operations after the project is closed
  • DHand over the system anyway and treat the funding problem as operations' concern
Show the answer

Answer: A. Transition includes ownership and budget for the run phase, so the gap is raised with the sponsor before handover. Handing over regardless, spending project funds on operations without approval or delaying silently leaves the value at risk.

S10At closure, the project folder holds approved documents, abandoned drafts and duplicate versions, and the project manager plans to archive the whole folder at once. What should be done first?

  • ADelete every file that does not appear on the closure checklist
  • BAsk each team member to keep a copy of their own files for future use
  • CArchive the whole folder exactly as it is, so that nothing is lost or altered
  • DCollect and audit the records, then archive the approved set in a controlled repository
Show the answer

Answer: D. Project records are collected and audited first and then archived in a controlled repository that others can reach, per retention policy. Archiving unreviewed files, deleting selectively or leaving copies with individuals defeats the purpose of archiving.

12.2 Recall Q&As

R1What does the ECO ask under Manage project closure?

Show the answer

Obtain stakeholder approval of completion, determine closure criteria, validate readiness for transition, and conclude closing activities (final lessons and retrospectives, procurement, financials, resources).

R2What is the purpose of Close Project or Phase?

Show the answer

To finalize all activities for successful and unsuccessful projects, phases, releases, iterations or contracts: archive information, complete planned work, release resources and confirm the extent to which value was achieved.

R3What are its key outputs?

Show the answer

Project document updates (lessons learned register), the final product, service or result transition, the final report and OPA updates.

R4What must be satisfied to meet the exit criteria in a predictive project?

Show the answer

Documents and deliverables updated and all issues resolved; measurable value delivered with a plan to maintain it; deliverables formally accepted; all costs charged and accounts closed; people released or reassigned; materials and facilities addressed; final reports prepared.

R5What does contract completion require?

Show the answer

Formal acceptance of the seller's work; open claims, guarantees and warranties finalized; records updated; invoices paid; relevant information archived; disputes resolved or referred to the dispute board.

R6What does adaptive closure of a release or iteration emphasize?

Show the answer

Prioritized items finished and acceptance criteria met, deliverables reviewed and accepted, no outstanding issues, knowledge-sharing sessions, retrospectives, and outstanding risks accepted or passed on.

R7What is the difference between verified and accepted deliverables?

Show the answer

Verified deliverables have passed quality control; accepted deliverables have been formally accepted by the customer or sponsor through validation.

R8What is the final product, service or result transition?

Show the answer

The handover of the delivered result (or a phase's intermediate result) to the group that will operate, maintain and support it.

R9When does a project usually end, according to the Standard?

Show the answer

When objectives are achieved; when they will not or cannot be met; when resources are exhausted; when the need disappears through changes in strategy, priorities or the external environment; or for legal, regulatory or compliance reasons.

R10What are the two early termination scenarios in Table 2-2?

Show the answer

Positive cause, the desired value impact has been achieved early; negative cause, the desired value impact is no longer achievable.

R11What must still happen when a project is terminated early?

Show the answer

Formal closure: document the delivered work, the reasons for termination and the lessons; settle contracts; release resources; archive records; communicate.

R12Who authorizes project completion?

Show the answer

The sponsor (or the governance body), on the project manager's recommendation.

R13What does the final report summarize?

Show the answer

Performance against scope, quality, cost and schedule objectives, validation of the final product, benefits and business needs achieved, and the risks and issues met and how they were handled.

R14What happens to benefits after closure?

Show the answer

The benefits owner named in the benefits management plan monitors, records and reports them over the planned timeframe; the business case and benefits plan are referenced after the project ends.

13Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
ECO task Manage project closure (Process Task 10): approval of completion, closure criteria, transition readiness, concluding activities
Purpose Finalize successful and unsuccessful projects, phases, releases, iterations, contracts; archive; release resources; confirm value achieved
Outputs Lessons learned register updates, final product or result transition, final report, OPA updates
Criteria Agreed early; acceptance, quality, administrative, contractual, transition, knowledge, value
Three "dones" Acceptance criteria (deliverable) · definition of done (item) · closure criteria (project or phase)
Acceptance Verified is not accepted: formal customer acceptance; silence is not acceptance; sponsor or governance authorizes completion
Phases Close with acceptance even if the sponsor continues; lessons feed the next phase
Readiness People practiced hands-on, documents, support, access, verification, open items transferred, owner accepts, communication
Knowledge Capture from departing people first; hands-on beats demos and manuals
Administrative Issues resolved, costs charged, accounts closed, people and resources released, records audited and archived
Contracts Seller's work accepted; claims, guarantees, warranties finalized; invoices paid; disputes resolved or referred; closed before the project
Lessons and OPAs Final lessons session; searchable repository; forward policy suggestions
Risks and issues Resolve or transfer with owners; record in the final report
Benefits Plan to maintain value; benefits owner and metrics; business case and benefits plan used after closure
Early termination Positive (value achieved) or negative (unachievable); still closes formally; document reasons and lessons; ignore sunk cost
Adaptive Finished items accepted, retrospective, unfinished backlog to the product owner when funding ends
